Graph neural networks (GNNs) have become a dominant paradigm for collaborative filtering (CF) by representing users and items as nodes in a bipartite interaction graph and propagating embeddings across edges. Early work such as Neural Graph Collaborative Filtering demonstrated that directly encoding the latent collaborative signal in the embedding propagation process yields substantial gains over traditional matrix‑factorization and feature‑based deep models, which often ignore higher‑order connectivity patterns [S2:c5f5f179d80a3bf9b4f29750283a87eaca42e91b]. By stacking graph convolution layers, these models capture multi‑hop user‑item relationships, establishing a new baseline for GNN‑based recommender systems.

Subsequent analyses have questioned which components of standard Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) are truly necessary for CF. LightGCN showed that the customary feature‑transformation matrices and nonlinear activations contribute little to recommendation performance; a simplified linear propagation scheme already attains state‑of‑the‑art results, and removing the extraneous operations even improves efficiency [S2:3024f58826a5bce3378af94f677e8fb90cbb49e0]. A complementary line of work revisited this observation by introducing a linear residual graph convolutional architecture that further eases training difficulty while preserving the expressive power of deep graph models for CF [S2:c9e432023a240b22f385cf1cc76ab75fbe084ee7].

Scalability to web‑scale datasets has also been a focal point. A production‑grade system deployed at Pinterest combined efficient random‑walk sampling with graph convolutions to generate embeddings for billions of items and hundreds of millions of users, demonstrating that GNN‑based recommenders can be made practical for industrial settings without sacrificing accuracy [S2:6c96c2d4a3fbd572fef2d59cb856521ee1746789]. To aid rapid model selection in new domains, researchers profiled the design space of GNN‑CF methods, systematically evaluating architectural dimensions such as aggregation functions, depth, and regularization; this study provides actionable guidelines for constructing high‑performing models under diverse data characteristics [S2:a2a42052eb8c0dd5ee339877b37f135fdfea00bd].

Comprehensive surveys have synthesized these advances, highlighting how GNNs enrich representation learning through contextual, higher‑order, and knowledge‑aware signals, and outlining open challenges such as cold‑start mitigation and heterogeneous graph integration [S2:1be97c1d9ace0363f8f612ca1be3d4fb33e177bb][S2:a669fc2d44fe5c49116a603f10d04a353468e190]. At the same time, a reproducibility‑driven analysis revealed that many reported gains of popular graph‑based CF models (e.g., NGCF, LightGCN, UltraGCN) are sensitive to experimental settings, underscoring the need for rigorous benchmarking and transparent code release to validate future contributions [S2:ac42cb67c0f022821e014cc8b7427e15fb4cd501]. Together, these works chart a clear trajectory: from establishing the efficacy of graph convolutions for CF, through simplifying and scaling the architectures, to critically assessing their empirical robustness.
